h1: Mobile canning services and when a small brewery should use one
title: Mobile Canning for a Small Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: When a small brewery should use a mobile canning service instead of buying a line, how the day works and what to check on quality and licences.
teaser: A canning line arrives on a truck, fills your beer and leaves by evening. The question is whether it suits your beer and your numbers.
standfirst: Buying a canning line is a big commitment for a brewery still learning what sells. A mobile canner offers a way to test packaged beer first. Here is how the day works and when it makes sense.
sections:
A mobile canning service brings a compact filler, seamer and usually a labeller or sleeve applicator to your brewery. You supply bright, carbonated beer at the right temperature, plus cans, ends and cartons. Their crew runs the line, you run the beer. By evening the kit is packed away and you have pallets of finished cans.

Mobile canning is well established in the United States, the UK and Australia. In India it is still rare. Availability depends heavily on where you are. Some contract packers and equipment suppliers offer canning runs, others do not. Ask before you build a plan around it.

• You want to test demand for packaged beer before investing in a line.
  • You package a few times a month, not every day.
  • Your floor space or power supply cannot take a permanent line yet.
  • You want seasonal or limited releases in cans without changing your core operation.

It makes less sense when you package most of your beer, need cans weekly or want full control over every variable. At that point a line of your own is usually cheaper per can. Our guide to kegs versus cans as a business choice covers that bigger decision.

The canner fills the can. The beer and its shelf life are still yours. The main risk is oxygen. Dissolved oxygen picked up during filling shortens shelf life sharply, especially in hoppy beers sitting in Indian heat. Ask the canner how they purge cans and what total package oxygen they usually achieve, then test it yourself if you can.

Seams matter as much as oxygen. A good crew does seam teardowns at the start of the run and at intervals, measuring the double seam with a micrometer or seam scope against the can maker's specification. Ask to see those records. A can that leaks slowly in a warm warehouse is a recall waiting to happen.

Have your beer ready: cold, carbonated to target and clear. Bright tank beer at about 0 to 2 °C fills with far less foaming than warm beer.

Canning is the easy part. Selling cans in India means label approval, excise registration of the brand and pack size, MRP declarations and the right licence to sell packaged beer off-premises. Many brewpub and microbrewery licences allow on-site consumption only. Check what your state permits before you order a single can. Rules vary by state and change.

Printed cans need minimum order quantities that can be large for a small brewery. Many start with plain cans and printed sleeves or labels, which suit short runs and seasonal beers.

A canning day starts early. The crew sets up the line, connects to your CO2, power and water and sanitises everything that touches beer. The first cans are usually checked for fill level, seam quality and oxygen before the run starts in earnest. Expect some beer and cans to be lost while the line settles. Your team keeps the bright tank at temperature and pressure, feeds empty cans and moves full cartons to the cold room as fast as they come off.

Plan the cold room space before the truck arrives. Pallets of warm cans stacked by the door at noon in summer undo much of the care taken on the filler. Taste a few cans from the start, middle and end of the run the next day and keep samples for shelf life checks.

Mobile canners usually charge per can or per run with a minimum. Add cans, ends, labels, cartons, your staff's time, beer lost at start-up and any rejects. Divide by good cans packed. Compare that figure with the per-can cost of owning a line, including depreciation, maintenance, spares and the labour to run it. Our beer packaging costs guide sets out the full list.

For many small breweries, mobile canning is a bridge: a way to learn about packaged beer without betting the business on it.

1. Confirm the licence and label position for packaged beer in your state.
  2. Agree volumes, minimums, dates and who supplies what.
  3. Check power, water, drainage and floor space for the line.
  4. Plan bright tank timing so the beer is ready and cold.
  5. Agree QC checks: oxygen, fill level, seams and carbonation.

If you are deciding whether packaged beer belongs in your plan at all, that decision needs the full picture of costs, pricing and distribution. It is worth learning with others who are making the same move.
faqs: Is mobile canning available in India?
It exists but is rare and depends on your location. Ask contract packers and equipment suppliers in your region what they currently offer.
Will mobile canning affect beer quality?
It can, mainly through oxygen pickup and seam quality. Ask the canner for oxygen and seam data and test the cans yourself.
Can a brewpub sell canned beer in India?
Many brewpub licences only allow on-site consumption. Selling packaged beer off-premises usually needs different permissions. Check your state's current rules.
